name: Greenish Grey
lede: Greenish Grey is a grey with a faint green cast, a name from the mineralogists' color charts of the 1790s that Syme fixed as number 15 in his 1821 edition of Werner's *Nomenclature of Colours*.

sections.title: A mineralogist's grey
sections.body:
The name comes from the world of mineral identification. Abraham Gottlob Werner published a list of 54 color terms in his 1774 textbook on the external characteristics of minerals, meant to be used with a set of mineral samples [1]. Claudine Picardet's French translation of 1790 added 17 colors to his list [2]. When Patrick Syme issued the 1821 edition, with painted swatches and an animal, a vegetable and a mineral example for each color, he marked greenish grey, his number 15, as coming from the Picardet system rather than from Werner's original list [3][4].

Baty's tables show the term in the charts of the 1790s and after, sitting between smoke grey and yellowish grey, with pearl grey next to it [5]. It was a working word, a way to say that a grey rock or feather leaned toward green.

sections.title: Syme's recipe and examples
sections.body:
Syme gave a recipe for each color. For greenish grey the base is ash grey, tinted with a touch of emerald green and lemon yellow and darkened with a small amount of black [4]. The examples he chose were the wing and quill feathers of the robin, the bark of the ash tree, and the rocks clay slate and wacke [4][3]. Baty's index of birds also places the pied flycatcher under this color [6].

The neighbors in his chart include [[yellowish-grey]], [[bluish-grey]] and [[pearl-grey]], and the lighter [[greenish-white]] and darker [[greenish-black]] sit on the same white-to-black ladder [5]. The same wording still turns up in mineral description: the Pigment Compendium says albite can be white, grey, greenish-grey or bluish-green [7].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The swatch here is a modern screen value, #8A8D84, close to a neutral: its Munsell notation is N 5.7, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files it under greenish gray, block 112 [8]. Syme's own swatch is an aged, hand-painted sample that can only be approximated on a screen [8]. The xkcd color survey of 2010 has its own greenish grey that is noticeably greener, #96AE8D [8]. Its contrast ratio is 3.37 against white and 6.22 against black [8]. Related colors include [[olive-grey]] and the broader [[grey]] family [8].

Gurney points out that a grey is judged by its surroundings. In a painting built on greens, the viewer's idea of neutral shifts a little toward green, so a greenish grey stroke can read as a plain grey while a true grey looks faintly reddish [9].

sections.title: Uniforms and offices
sections.body: Pastoureau mentions the greenish gray of German uniforms in the two world wars, *feldgrau*, and says it left fashion designers cold [10]. He ties it to what he calls administrative green: a drab, grayish green that spread through offices, train stations and post offices from the 1900s and that he calls the emblematic color of bureaucracy [10]. By his account it stayed popular until the 1970s [10]. These are descriptions of related drab greens, not measurements of this swatch.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Greenish Grey is common in painting [11]. It appears in 1,049 of 23,781 paintings in our archive, 4.41 per cent, and is more common than 84 per cent of the named colors [11]. It peaks in the 1900s, when 3.9 per cent of the 1,674 paintings we hold from that century have it, 1.6 times the rate of the same museums' baseline [11]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light, in 46 per cent of the 590 paintings where the within-painting lens finds it [11].

The painter most devoted to it is Eugène Boudin, with the color in 9 of 33 works here, 7.0 times the baseline; Matisse has it in 10 of 50 [11]. It shares canvases with Deep Neutral Grey and Agate Grey more than chance would predict [11]. The earliest dated match is [[painting:cma-145719|a work by Devachandra]] of 1279, and the latest is [[painting:commons-Q27966072|a painting of 1950]] [11]. The 1279 match is 542 years before Syme's name, so it is a look-alike hue in an aged photograph, not evidence of any pigment [11]. Every number here is as photographed.
